title: First-issued USGS ShakeMap uncertainties were too narrow for PGA and PGV at stations that later versions added (3,547 events, 2018-2026); MMI intervals were approximately calibrated
abstract: Question: are the standard deviations that USGS ShakeMap 4 issues in its first map calibrated against shaking that the map did not use? Approach: we read all archived ShakeMap versions in ComCat for 10,916 events (2018-2026; M 3.5 or more near the United States, M 5.5 or more worldwide). For each event we compared the first issued version (median 14 minutes after origin) with seismic stations and Did You Feel It? cells that only a later version of the same stream used. We wrote the plan before we downloaded station data. Results: in 3,547 events, only 69.9% (95% CI 68.8-70.9%) of 72,048 station PGA values were inside the stated 90% interval; PGV gave 73.6% and SA(1.0 s) 71.6%. The maps were also too high: for 1,913 maps without stations the mean event term was -0.42 ln units. The observed between-event standard deviation of ln PGA was 0.65 (0.62-0.68), but ShakeMap stated 0.43; after removal of regional means it was 0.58. Bias depended on region: -1.0 in Hawaii and Texas, -0.6 in Puerto Rico, -0.25 for global events, and +0.26 in southern California. Versions within 60 minutes or 24 hours were not better (74% and 72%). MMI intervals were approximately calibrated: 90.9% at seismic stations and 92.2% for 150,558 new DYFI cells, because the stated MMI spread includes conversion scatter. An exploratory bias-and-scale recalibration fitted on 2018-2022 raised 2023-2026 PGA coverage from 65.9% to 90.3% and increased log predictive density by 0.89 per station. Limitations: late stations are not a random sample, archived amplitudes contain some errors, and the recalibration is retrospective.
